meta.title: Colombian Elections
sources: Wikipedia: Colombian presidential and parliamentary election articles 1825-2026
Registraduria Nacional del Estado Civil figures as reported there

presEras.label: Election by the colleges
presEras.blurb: For its first thirty years the republic chose presidents through provincial electoral colleges and, when they failed to produce a majority, through congress. The figures here are the electors' votes, not a popular ballot, and the men in them are the founders: Bolívar, Santander, Páez, Márquez, Mosquera.

presEras.label: The sovereign states
presEras.blurb: Under the federal constitutions of 1858 and 1863 the president was chosen by the nine states, each casting one vote, and a candidate needed five. These contests have no popular vote at all and appear here with the winner and no figures, because the article records states won rather than ballots cast. Presidential terms ran two years and the country fought several civil wars across the period.

presEras.label: Regeneration and the Conservative hegemony
presEras.blurb: Núñez's Regeneration replaced the federal republic with a centralised one in 1886 and the Conservatives held the presidency for forty-four years. The Thousand Days' War and the loss of Panama fall inside the period, and it ends when the Conservatives split in 1930 and let Olaya Herrera through on 45%.

presEras.label: The Liberal Republic and the Violencia
presEras.blurb: Sixteen years of Liberal presidents, then the split of 1946 that let the Conservatives back in on a minority, then the assassination of Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in April 1948 and the undeclared civil war that killed perhaps two hundred thousand people. The 1949 election was contested by one candidate because the Liberals refused to take part in it.

presEras.label: The National Front
presEras.blurb: The parties agreed in 1957 to alternate the presidency between them for sixteen years and to divide every elected body equally. Four presidents were elected under it, each of them the only candidate his half of the pact could nominate. The last of the four contests, in 1970, was won by 1.6 points against a former dictator whose supporters believed the count had been altered, and a guerrilla movement took its name from the date.

presEras.label: The open contest
presEras.blurb: The pact lapsed and the presidency became a real two-party race again, decided in one round by simple plurality. Three presidential candidates were murdered in the run-up to the 1990 election.

presEras.label: Two rounds
presEras.blurb: The 1991 constitution introduced a runoff, and every election since has gone to one. It has produced the widest swings in Colombian politics: Uribe's outright first-round win in 2002, the peace referendum that followed Santos, Gustavo Petro as the first left-wing president in 2022, and in June 2026 Abelardo de la Espriella beating Iván Cepeda by less than a point.

legEras.label: The republic's first congress
legEras.blurb: Gran Colombia's congress and presidency were chosen by provincial electoral colleges rather than by voters, and the record of the period that survives in this atlas is a single election. The century that followed had congressional elections too; the articles for them are not in the source used here, which is why the legislative series restarts in 1931.

legEras.label: The Liberal Republic
legEras.blurb: The Liberals took congress in 1931 after fifty years of Conservative hegemony and held it at every election for eighteen years, with universal male suffrage from 1936 and majorities above 60%. The period ends badly: Gaitán's murder in 1948, the Violencia that followed, and the closure of congress by President Gómez in 1949.

legEras.label: Rojas and the junta
legEras.blurb: Congress was shut in November 1949 and the elections of 1951 and 1953 were contested by the Conservatives alone, the Liberals having withdrawn. General Rojas Pinilla took power in 1953 and the Constituent Assembly that confirmed him was appointed rather than elected.

legEras.label: The National Front
legEras.blurb: The two parties ended the Violencia by agreeing to share everything: the seats in congress were split equally between Liberals and Conservatives for sixteen years, and voters chose between factions of their own party rather than between parties. The tables here show that, faction by faction. Everyone outside the pact, including the ANAPO movement that grew to a fifth of the vote, could win support but not seats.

legEras.label: After the pact
legEras.blurb: Competition returned and the Liberals won every congressional election of the period, usually with a majority of the Senate. It was also the most violent electoral era in Colombian history: the Unión Patriótica, formed out of the 1985 peace talks, had thousands of its members and two of its presidential candidates murdered.

legEras.label: The 1991 constitution
legEras.blurb: The new constitution created a 100-seat Senate elected as a single national district, which was meant to break the regional machines and instead produced hundreds of personal lists. The 2003 reform imposed a threshold and forced parties to run one list each, cutting the field from sixty-odd parties to about twenty. In 2026 the Historic Pact topped the Senate poll with 25 of the 100 elected seats, the best result the Colombian left has recorded.
